guides.title: Carpet Plants Without CO2: Low-Tech Aquarium Carpet Guide
guides.description: Achieve a lush aquarium carpet without CO2 injection. Discover the best low-tech plants, essential gear, and crucial care tips for success.

faq.q: What is the easiest carpet plant without CO2?
faq.a: Dwarf Sagittaria (*Sagittaria subulata 'Dwarf'*) is generally considered the easiest. It's hardy, spreads reliably by runners, and tolerates a wide range of water parameters and light conditions.

faq.q: How long does it take to carpet a tank without CO2?
faq.a: Expect it to take significantly longer than with CO2. Depending on the plant species and tank conditions, a full carpet can take anywhere from 3 to 6 months, or even longer for very slow growers like Cryptocoryne parva or Marsilea hirsuta.

faq.q: Do I need special lighting for a low-tech carpet?
faq.a: Yes, good quality LED lighting is crucial. While you don't need extremely high light like a CO2-injected tank, you need consistent, medium-intensity light to promote horizontal growth. Lights like the Aurora 48 LED or Aurora Smart 78 provide the necessary spectrum and intensity.

faq.q: Can Monte Carlo carpet without CO2?
faq.a: Monte Carlo (*Micranthemum 'Monte Carlo'*) can carpet without CO2, but it's challenging. It requires high light, a nutrient-rich substrate, and consistent liquid fertilisation. Growth will be very slow, and it's more prone to algae than other low-tech options. It's not recommended for beginners trying a low-tech carpet.

guides.title: Best Light for Planted Tank: A Guide to Strong Plant Growth
guides.description: Find the best light for your planted aquarium. Learn about PAR, spectrum, and intensity to grow thriving plants without algae. Get honest recommendations.

faq.q: How many hours a day should I run my planted tank light?
faq.a: Start with 6-8 hours daily. If you see algae, reduce the duration. If plants look leggy or pale, increase it slowly. Consistency with a timer is key.

faq.q: Do I need a "full spectrum" light?
faq.a: "Full spectrum" is a common marketing term. What matters is that the light provides sufficient red and blue wavelengths for plant photosynthesis. Many good LED lights achieve this without being labeled "full spectrum."

faq.q: What is PAR and why is it important?
faq.a: PAR (Photosynthetically Active Radiation) measures the light energy plants actually use for photosynthesis. It's a more accurate way to gauge a light's effectiveness for plant growth than lumens or watts.

faq.q: Is more powerful light always better for plants?
faq.a: No. Too much light without adequate CO2 and nutrients will cause severe algae problems, not better plant growth. Match light intensity to your plants' needs and your tank's CO2 setup.
